- Acute-onset, non-bloody, watery diarrhea (9 episodes over 48 hours) — classic presentation of CDI  
- Lower abdominal cramping — common symptom in CDI  
- Recent levofloxacin use for pneumonia — major risk factor for CDI (fluoroquinolones are high-risk antibiotics)  
- Neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis (WBC 13,400/mm³) — frequently observed in CDI, even in absence of fever  
- No fever, vomiting, hematochezia, or systemic alarm features — aligns with mild-to-moderate CDI (not fulminant)  
- *C. difficile* toxin A/B testing ordered — clinician’s diagnostic priority reflects high pretest probability  
- No epidemiologic risk factors for other enteric pathogens — increases relative likelihood of CDI  

[GAPS]  
- *C. difficile* toxin A/B (or PCR) result — definitive confirmation pending  
- Stool GDH (glutamate dehydrogenase) result — if positive, supports CDI even if toxin is negative (due to lower sensitivity of toxin-only assays)  
- Stool white blood cells (WBCs) or lactoferrin — would support inflammatory diarrhea but not specified  
- Duration of antibiotic exposure and exact timing relative to diarrhea onset — affects strength of temporal association  
- Renal function (e.g., creatinine) and electrolytes — needed to assess severity/dehydration but not yet obtained  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
*Clostridioides difficile* infection
